text.text:
Some of the companies that announced they're "banning" AI agents:
United Airlines
Booking
Amazon
eBay
JPMorgan Chase
Bank of America
Yelp

I say "banning" because while they're trying to keep AI agents out, those same agents are only getting better at bypassing the barriers designed to stop them.

You are soon going to see Proof of Human layers verifying that important actions are authorized by a person, rather than an unattested agent.

Trying to ban bots will always be a losing game of whack-a-mole. My take? Find ways to let approved agents do the work but empower humans to stay in control when it matters.

text.text:
Bank of America knew for years that its monitoring wasn’t escalating potentially suspicious activity to investigators. Almost two years after signing an OCC order to fix it, regulators say the problems persisted.
The result: a penalty of more than $1.21 billion, and over $5 billion in suspicious transactions reported late to FinCEN.
In Part 1 of my series Beyond the Checklist, I break down three lessons from the case:
  1. A monitoring system is only as good as the controls behind it
  2. Customer due diligence doesn’t end at onboarding
  3. Spotting suspicious activity is only half the job
I’m early in my AML/KYC journey, so I’d value your perspective. For those working in this field: when a control weakness is known, what makes it get fixed rather than documented?

subDescription.accessibilityText: 2 weeks ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

text.text:
Would you hand your house keys to a stranger who promised to “just tidy up”? 🔑
No? Then here’s a plot twist:
Some people are doing exactly that… with their bank accounts. 😅

Big U.S. banks recently noticed something unusual inside customer accounts. 
Not hackers. Not fraudsters.
AI assistants. 
Logging in with the customer’s own username and password.

Bank of America even emailed customers with a polite but firm message: please don’t share your banking password with your AI agent. And if you do, you’re responsible for what it does.

So let’s simplify today’s concept: AI Agents 🤖

Think of AI in two flavours:
💬 The Chatbot = a very smart friend on the phone.
It can tell you which bill to pay. But you still pay it.
🦾 The Agent = a friend with your keys.
It doesn’t just advise. It acts: logs in, clicks buttons, moves money.

That’s a huge leap. Because when an agent acts, three awkward questions pop up:
1️⃣ Who is actually logged in? Some banks can’t easily tell you apart from your AI.
2️⃣ Who said yes? Did you approve that transfer, or did your agent “assume”?
3️⃣ Who pays if it goes wrong? (Spoiler: right now, often you.)

So how are banks responding?

JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Schwab have all drawn a similar line:
👀 AI agents can look (check balances, read statements)
🚫 AI agents can’t move money

Schwab says it’s blocking unauthorised agents more than ten times a week. Jamie Dimon summed up the worry neatly: you don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them.

My favourite way to picture the banks’ approach is the valet key 🚗
It starts the car and parks it. But it can’t open the glovebox or the boot.
Limited access. Clear boundaries. A human still holds the master key.

The lesson for all of us:
AI agents are coming to finance. That’s not the debate anymore.
The real question is: how much of the key do we hand over, and to whom?

Drop your comments on which AI concept I should untangle next!


#AIAgents #AIinFinance #AIGovernance #FinTech #ResponsibleAI #Banking
